chapter_note.about: A support vector machine separates two classes with the straight boundary that leaves the widest empty street between them. Only the points touching the street, the support vectors, decide where the boundary goes. This chapter covers the distance of a point from a plane, the hard-margin problem, support vectors, the dual weights, when no straight line can work, the soft margin with its penalty C, and kernels that bend the boundary.

concept_map.title: The score f(x) and distance to the plane
concept_map.one_line: The score is w.x + b. The distance is the score divided by the length of w.

concept_map.title: Hard margin: the widest street
concept_map.one_line: Minimise half of |w|^2 with every y f at least 1. The street is 2/|w| wide.

concept_map.title: Support vectors
concept_map.one_line: Points with y f exactly 1 hold the plane. Any other point can go.

concept_map.title: Dual and KKT conditions
concept_map.one_line: w is a weighted sum of support vectors. The weights balance and add up to |w|^2.

concept_map.title: Linear separability and XOR
concept_map.one_line: A hard margin needs the two classes to be apart. Overlapping rubber bands, as in XOR, rule it out.

concept_map.title: Soft margin and C
concept_map.one_line: Pay C per unit of slack. Big C gives a narrow street and small C a wide one.

concept_map.title: Kernels and feature maps
concept_map.one_line: Lift the data and use K(x,z) = phi(x).phi(z) to get a curved boundary.

concept_map.title: Valid kernels
concept_map.one_line: Symmetric with a PSD Gram matrix. Sums and products are safe. A difference is not.

chapter_note.simple: An SVM is a road-builder. It looks at two groups of points and builds the widest straight road between them. Only the points right at the kerb decide where the road goes, and everyone else could leave without changing it. If the groups are mixed up, it can allow a few trespassers for a fine, or lift the points into a higher space where a straight road does fit. Kernels let it do the lifting cheaply. In exam words: the SVM maximises the margin $2/\|w\|$, depends only on the support vectors, and uses a soft margin (penalty $C$) or a kernel when the data are not linearly separable.

cards.title: The score f(x) and distance to the plane
cards.simple: Picture a straight fence across a field. Everyone on one side is labelled yes and everyone on the other side is labelled no. The fence has an equation, and plugging a person's position into it gives a score. The score is positive on the yes side, negative on the no side, and zero right on the fence. The score is not metres, though. Think of a ramp: the steeper the ramp, the faster the height climbs per step, so height divided by steepness gives the steps walked. In exam words: the distance is $|w^\top x+b|/\|w\|$.
cards.idea: A linear classifier draws one straight line (a flat plane in more dimensions) between the classes. Each point gets a **score** $f(x)=w^\top x+b$. The sign of the score is the predicted class. The size of the score tells you how far the point is from the line, but only after you divide by the length of $w$.
cards.definition:
$$f(x)=w^\top x+b,\qquad \text{distance of }x=\frac{|f(x)|}{\|w\|},\qquad \|w\|=\sqrt{w_1^2+w_2^2+\cdots}$$

Symbols: $w$ is the weight vector. It points at a right angle to the plane, toward the positive side. $b$ is the offset. The plane is the set of points with $f(x)=0$. $\|w\|$ is the length of $w$.
cards.intuition_full: Why divide by $\|w\|$? Take any plane and multiply both $w$ and $b$ by 10. The plane has not moved, but every score is now 10 times bigger. So the raw score cannot be a distance. Think of $f$ as the height of a tilted ramp that is flat (height 0) along the plane. Walk one step straight away from the plane and the height rises by exactly $\|w\|$. A steeper ramp has a bigger $\|w\|$ and the same step gives a bigger height. So height divided by steepness is the number of steps walked, which is the distance. Why does $w$ point at a right angle to the plane? Take two points $p$ and $q$ on the plane. Then $w^\top p+b=0$ and $w^\top q+b=0$, so $w^\top(p-q)=0$. A dot product of zero means the two vectors are perpendicular, and $p-q$ runs along the plane.

examples.setup: A plane has $w=(5,12)$ and $b=-30$. Find the score and the distance of $A=(4,3)$ and $B=(1,1)$.
steps: $A=(4,3)$: $f(A)=5\cdot4+12\cdot3-30=20+36-30=26$. It is positive, so $A$ is on the $+$ side.
Distance of $A$: $|26|/13=2$.
$B=(1,1)$: $f(B)=5+12-30=-13$. It is negative, so $B$ is on the $-$ side. Distance: $|-13|/13=1$.
$A$ is 2 away on the $+$ side and $B$ is 1 away on the $-$ side. The score 26 is not the distance. The distance is the score divided by 13.
examples.answer: $A$: $f=26$, distance 2, class $+$. $B$: $f=-13$, distance 1, class $-$.

examples.setup: Plane $P_1$ has $w=(1,1)$, $b=-3$. Plane $P_2$ has $w=(2,2)$, $b=-6$. For $x=(3,2)$, compare the scores and the distances.
steps: $P_1$: $f=3+2-3=2$. $\|w\|=\sqrt2$. Distance $2/\sqrt2=\sqrt2\approx1.414$.
The scores differ (2 and 4) but the distances agree. $P_2$ is $P_1$ with $w$ and $b$ doubled, so it is the same plane.
examples.answer: Scores 2 and 4, distance $\sqrt2$ for both. The score depends on how $w$ is scaled. The distance does not. A question that compares raw scores across two scalings is a trap.

examples.setup: A plane has $w=(8,15)$ and $b=-34$. How far is the origin from it?
steps: The origin makes every term $w_ix_i$ zero, so $f(0)=b=-34$.
Distance $=|-34|/17=2$. The score is negative, so the origin is on the $-$ side.
examples.answer: The origin is 2 units from the plane. In general the origin's distance is $|b|/\|w\|$.

cards.why: Every SVM question measures a distance to a plane, so this is the first tool. The margin on the next card is built from it. In GATE: given $w$ and $b$, find the distance of a point or say which side it is on.
how: Write the score $f(x)=w^\top x+b$ and put the point in.
The sign of $f$ is the class.
Find $\|w\|=\sqrt{\text{sum of squares of the entries}}$.
Divide $|f|$ by $\|w\|$ for the distance.
cards.mistake: Reading the score $f(x)$ as the distance. The score changes when you scale $w$ and $b$, but the plane does not move. Always divide by $\|w\|$ first.
edge_cases: $f(x)=0$ means the point is on the plane and its distance is 0.
The origin has $f(0)=b$, so its distance is $|b|/\|w\|$.
Multiplying $w$ and $b$ by $c>0$ multiplies every score by $c$ but leaves the plane, the distances and the classes unchanged.
Multiplying by a negative number gives the same plane with the two sides swapped.
connections: Foundations: Algebra covers the squares, square roots and absolute value used here.
Linear algebra: Vector spaces covers the length (norm) of a vector.
Next card: the margin is twice the distance of the closest point.

check.q: $w=(0,5)$ and $b=-10$. What is the distance of $(7,4)$ from the plane?
check.a: $f=0\cdot7+5\cdot4-10=10$ and $\|w\|=5$, so the distance is $10/5=2$. (The plane is the horizontal line $x_2=2$ and the point is 2 above it.)

check.q: You multiply $w$ and $b$ by 3. What happens to the score, the distance and the class of a point?
check.a: The score becomes 3 times bigger. The distance and the class stay the same, because $\|w\|$ also becomes 3 times bigger.

check.q: A point has score $-7$ and $\|w\|=7$. Which side is it on and how far away?
check.a: The negative side, at distance $7/7=1$.

cards.title: Hard margin: the widest street
cards.simple: Two groups of kids stand in a playground and you must paint a line between them. You could paint it close to one group, or at any angle. The SVM paints it so the empty strip around the line is as wide as it can be, like the widest road that fits between two neighbourhoods. The road edges touch the nearest kid on each side. A wide road means a new kid is less likely to land on the wrong side. In exam words: maximise the margin $2/\|w\|$, which means minimise $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ while every $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1$.
cards.idea: Many lines can separate two classes. The SVM picks the one with the widest empty street between them. The street edges are two parallel planes, $f=+1$ and $f=-1$. A shorter $w$ makes a wider street, so the SVM makes $w$ as short as possible while keeping every point on its own side of the street.
cards.definition:
$$\min_{w,b}\ \tfrac12\|w\|^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i\,(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1\ \text{ for every point } i,\qquad \text{margin width}=\frac{2}{\|w\|}$$

Symbols: $y_i$ is the label, $+1$ or $-1$. The product $y_if(x_i)$ is positive when the point is on its correct side. The condition says it is at least 1, so no point is inside the street. The margin width is the gap between the planes $f=+1$ and $f=-1$.
cards.intuition_full: Why does a shorter $w$ give a wider street? The score $f$ climbs from 0 at the middle plane to 1 at the street edge. Each step you walk away from the plane raises $f$ by $\|w\|$. A small $\|w\|$ is a gentle ramp, so you must walk far to reach height 1. The edge is far away, so the street is wide. Why the number 1? Only the sign of $f$ matters for classifying, so we are free to rescale $(w,b)$. We fix the scale by demanding that the closest points reach exactly $\pm1$. That leaves one answer. Why $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ and not $\|w\|$? Both are smallest at the same $w$. The square has no square root, so the algebra and the dual on the next cards come out clean.

examples.setup: Two training points: class $+1$ at $(4,6)$ and class $-1$ at $(1,2)$. Find $w$, $b$ and the margin width of the hard-margin SVM.
steps: The constraints are $f(4,6)\ge1$ and $f(1,2)\le-1$. The best plane makes both exactly tight.
$w$ points along the difference $d=(4,6)-(1,2)=(3,4)$. Its length is $|d|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$.
Across a gap of 5, $f$ must rise from $-1$ to $+1$, a rise of 2. The rise per unit step is $\|w\|$, so $\|w\|=2/5=0.4$. Margin width $=2/0.4=5$.
examples.answer: $w=(0.24,0.32)$, $b=-1.88$, margin width $5$. With one point per class the margin is simply the distance between the two points.

examples.setup: Data: class $+1$ at $(3,0),(6,1),(8,1)$ and class $-1$ at $(4,1),(1,2),(0,0)$. Someone claims the hard-margin solution is $w=(1,-3)$, $b=-2$. Check it and find the margin.
steps: Every $y f\ge1$, so the plane is feasible. Three points are exactly at 1, namely $(3,0)$, $(6,1)$ and $(4,1)$. Shrinking $w$ would push one of them below 1.
$\|w\|=\sqrt{1+9}=\sqrt{10}$, so the margin is $2/\sqrt{10}\approx0.632$.
examples.answer: The claim holds. Margin $2/\sqrt{10}\approx0.632$ and the points on the margin are $(3,0)$, $(6,1)$, $(4,1)$. The three far points have $y f>1$.

examples.setup: Same data. A second candidate is $w=(2,-6)$, $b=-4$. Is it feasible, and is it the SVM answer?
steps: This is the first candidate with $w$ and $b$ doubled, so every $y f$ doubles: $2,2,6,2,14,4$. All are at least 1, so it is feasible.
Its length is $\|w\|=\sqrt{4+36}=\sqrt{40}\approx6.32$, twice the old one. The margin is $2/6.32\approx0.316$, half as wide.
examples.answer: Feasible but not the SVM answer. Both candidates separate the data, and the SVM wants the one with the smallest $\|w\|$. Feasible does not mean optimal.

cards.why: This is the problem an SVM solves. Every later card (support vectors, the dual, the soft margin) is a view of it or a change to it. In GATE: find $w$, $b$ and the margin for a tiny 2D set, usually by guessing from the closest opposite pair and checking.
how: Find the closest points of opposite classes. They set the direction of $w$.
Scale $w$ so that $f$ rises by 2 across their gap. That gives $\|w\|$.
Margin width $=2/\|w\|$. Get $b$ from one tight point.
Check that every other point has $y f\ge1$.
cards.mistake: Using $1/\|w\|$ as the margin width. $1/\|w\|$ is the distance from the middle plane to the nearest point. The whole street is twice that, $2/\|w\|$.
edge_cases: One point per class: the plane is the perpendicular bisector and the margin is the distance between the points.
If no plane separates the classes, no $(w,b)$ satisfies all the constraints. The hard-margin problem has no answer.
The right side of the constraint is 1, not 0. That is what fixes the scale of $w$.
Adding a point that already has $y f>1$ changes nothing.
connections: Previous card: the distance of a point to the plane is $|f|/\|w\|$.
Next card: the points sitting exactly on $f=\pm1$ are the support vectors.
Ridge regression also minimises $\|w\|^2$, as a penalty. Foundations: Algebra covers the squares and ratios here.

check.q: A hard-margin SVM has $\|w\|=0.5$. What is the margin width?
Only two points: $+1$ at $(0,0)$ and $-1$ at $(0,6)$. What are the margin width, $w$ and $b$?
check.a: The distance between them is 6, so the margin is 6 and $\|w\|=2/6=1/3$. $w$ points from the $-$ point to the $+$ point, which is downward, so $w=(0,-1/3)$. Then $f(0,0)=b=1$. Check: $f(0,6)=-2+1=-1$.

check.q: A student writes margin $=1/\|w\|$. What does $1/\|w\|$ actually measure?
check.a: The distance from the middle plane to the closest point, which is half the street.

cards.title: Support vectors
cards.simple: Imagine sliding a flat board between two groups of nails hammered into a table. You push until the board touches the nearest nails on each side. Those touching nails hold the board in place, and the far nails never touch it. Pull a far nail out and the board stays put. Move a touching nail and the board must move. In exam words: support vectors are the training points with $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)=1$, and the plane depends only on them.
cards.idea: A **support vector** is a training point that sits exactly on the edge of the street, where $y\,f(x)=1$. These points hold the plane in place. Every other point has room to spare, so you could delete all of them and the SVM would draw the same plane.
cards.definition:
$$\text{support vector:}\ \ y_i\,(w^\top x_i+b)=1\qquad\qquad \text{any other point:}\ \ y_i\,(w^\top x_i+b)>1$$

Symbols: $y_i f(x_i)$ is the signed score of point $i$. It is 1 for a point on the street edge and larger for a point farther away on its correct side. In a hard-margin SVM no point has a value below 1.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the plane as a rigid board pushed between two groups of nails. It stops when it touches the nearest nails on each side. Those touching nails are the only ones that stop it. A nail far from the board never touches it, so removing that nail changes nothing. Move a touching nail and the board has to tilt or slide. In the maths, the optimum is decided by the constraints that are exactly tight ($y f=1$). A loose constraint ($y f>1$) could be thrown away and the optimum would not notice. This is why the SVM is compact: out of thousands of points it may keep only a handful. A point being correctly classified is far from enough. The name 'support' means the point helps hold up the plane. It does not mean the point is typical of its class or far from the plane.

examples.setup: A trained hard-margin SVM has $w=(1,-2)$ and $b=-1$. The data are $+1$ at $(4,1),(6,2),(7,1)$ and $-1$ at $(4,2),(2,3),(1,1)$. Which points are support vectors?
steps: The score is $f(x)=x_1-2x_2-1$. For each point compute $y\cdot f$. Support vectors are the ones that give exactly 1.
Exactly 1: $(4,1)$, $(6,2)$ and $(4,2)$. These are the support vectors. $(7,1)$, $(2,3)$ and $(1,1)$ have $yf>1$.
Delete the three far points and retrain. The three constraints that were tight are still there, so the plane and the margin do not change.
examples.answer: Three support vectors: $(4,1)$, $(6,2)$ and $(4,2)$. The other three points can be deleted without changing the plane.

examples.setup: Same data and plane. Which single change moves the hyperplane? (A) delete $(7,1)$. (B) delete $(2,3)$. (C) delete $(6,2)$. (D) move $(7,1)$ to $(9,1)$.
steps: $(7,1)$ has $yf=4>1$. It is not a support vector, so deleting it changes nothing. (A) no.
$(2,3)$ has $yf=5>1$. Deleting it changes nothing. (B) no.
Moving $(7,1)$ to $(9,1)$ gives $yf=9-2-1=6$. It is still far outside the street, so the plane stays. (D) no.

$(6,2)$ has $yf=1$, so it is a support vector. Without it the positive class is only $(4,1)$ and $(7,1)$, and the nearest positive to $(4,2)$ is $(4,1)$ straight below it. The best plane tilts to $\tfrac23x_1-2x_2+\tfrac13=0$. (C) yes.
examples.answer: Only (C). A point that is not a support vector can be deleted or moved around outside the street without moving the plane.

examples.setup: Data: $+1$ at $(3,2),(2,3),(5,4)$ and $-1$ at $(2,1),(1,2),(1,1)$. The plane is $x_1+x_2-4=0$. Four points sit on the margin. Delete $(2,1)$ and retrain. Does the plane move?
steps: $f=x_1+x_2-4$ gives $yf=1,1,5$ for the positives and $1,1,2$ for the negatives. So $(3,2),(2,3),(2,1),(1,2)$ are all on the margin.
After deleting $(2,1)$ the closest opposite pair is $(2,3)$ and $(1,2)$. Their gap is $(1,1)$, so $w$ still points along $(1,1)$ and the plane is still $x_1+x_2=4$.
$(2,1)$ was on the margin, but $(3,2)$, $(2,3)$ and $(1,2)$ already pin the same plane.
examples.answer: No, the plane does not move. Deleting a support vector usually moves the plane, but not when other margin points hold it in the same place. The safe rule is that deleting or moving a non-support vector never changes the plane.

cards.why: The SVM is compact because it keeps only these points. They are also what exam questions ask for: identify them, count them, or say what happens when points are deleted. In GATE: given a small 2D set, find which points lie on the margin.
how: Get $w$ and $b$ (from the question, or by guessing from the closest opposite pair).
Compute $y\cdot f(x)$ for every point.
Points with exactly 1 are the support vectors.
A far point with $yf>1$ cannot move the plane.

cards.what_full:
A **support vector** is a training point that sits exactly on the edge of the street, where $y\,f(x)=1$. These points hold the plane in place. Every other point has room to spare, so you could delete all of them and the SVM would draw the same plane.

$$\text{support vector:}\ \ y_i\,(w^\top x_i+b)=1\qquad\qquad \text{any other point:}\ \ y_i\,(w^\top x_i+b)>1$$

Symbols: $y_i f(x_i)$ is the signed score of point $i$. It is 1 for a point on the street edge and larger for a point farther away on its correct side. In a hard-margin SVM no point has a value below 1.

**Worked example.** A trained hard-margin SVM has $w=(1,-2)$ and $b=-1$. The data are $+1$ at $(4,1),(6,2),(7,1)$ and $-1$ at $(4,2),(2,3),(1,1)$. Which points are support vectors?

1. The score is $f(x)=x_1-2x_2-1$. For each point compute $y\cdot f$. Support vectors are the ones that give exactly 1.
2. Class $+1$: $f(4,1)=4-2-1=1$, $f(6,2)=6-4-1=1$, $f(7,1)=7-2-1=4$. With $y=+1$: $yf=1,1,4$.
3. Class $-1$: $f(4,2)=4-4-1=-1$, $f(2,3)=2-6-1=-5$, $f(1,1)=1-2-1=-2$. Multiply by $y=-1$: $yf=1,5,2$.
4. Exactly 1: $(4,1)$, $(6,2)$ and $(4,2)$. These are the support vectors. $(7,1)$, $(2,3)$ and $(1,1)$ have $yf>1$.
5. Delete the three far points and retrain. The three constraints that were tight are still there, so the plane and the margin do not change.

**Answer:** Three support vectors: $(4,1)$, $(6,2)$ and $(4,2)$. The other three points can be deleted without changing the plane.

**Check yourself:** A trained SVM has $w=(1,0)$ and $b=-3$. Points: $(4,5)$ and $(5,0)$ in class $+1$, $(2,2)$ and $(0,3)$ in class $-1$. Which are support vectors?

*Answer:* $yf$ is $4-3=1$, $5-3=2$, $-(2-3)=1$ and $-(0-3)=3$. So $(4,5)$ and $(2,2)$ are support vectors.

cards.title: Dual and KKT conditions
cards.simple: Think of a tug-of-war. The support vectors are the players. Each player pulls toward their own class with some strength. The rope only settles where the pull from the two teams is equal, so the total strength of the + team equals the total strength of the - team. Players who are not touching the rope pull with strength zero. Add up each player's pull in their own direction and you get the weight vector $w$. In exam words: $w=\sum\alpha_iy_ix_i$, $\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$ and $\alpha_i>0$ only on support vectors.
cards.idea: The dual view builds the plane from the training points themselves. Each point gets a **weight** $\alpha_i\ge0$. The weight vector is the weighted sum of the points, with $+$ for class $+1$ and $-$ for class $-1$. The weights of the two classes must balance. Only support vectors get a weight above zero.
cards.definition:
$$w=\sum_i\alpha_i\,y_i\,x_i,\qquad \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0,\qquad \alpha_i\ge0,\qquad \alpha_i\,\big(y_if(x_i)-1\big)=0,\qquad \sum_i\alpha_i=\|w\|^2$$

Symbols: $\alpha_i$ is the weight of point $i$. The fourth condition (complementary slackness) says that either $\alpha_i=0$ or $y_if(x_i)=1$, so only margin points can have $\alpha_i>0$. The last equality holds at the hard-margin optimum.
cards.intuition_full: Where does $w=\sum\alpha_iy_ix_i$ come from? A support vector is a constraint that is exactly tight. Think of each tight constraint as pushing on the plane with a force $\alpha_i$. The best plane is where all pushes balance. Two things must balance. The pushes add up to $w$, which is the first formula. And the total push from the $+$ side equals the total push from the $-$ side, which is $\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$. If it did not, the plane would slide. A loose constraint ($y_if>1$) pushes with force zero, which is complementary slackness. Why is $\sum\alpha_i=\|w\|^2$? Take $\|w\|^2=w^\top w$ and replace one $w$ by its sum: $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,(w^\top x_i)$. Now $w^\top x_i=f(x_i)-b$, so this is $\sum_i\alpha_iy_if(x_i)-b\sum_i\alpha_iy_i$. For a support vector $y_if(x_i)=1$, and the balance condition makes the second sum 0. What is left is $\sum_i\alpha_i$.

examples.setup: A trained hard-margin SVM has support vectors $x_1=(2,2)$ and $x_2=(4,1)$ in class $+1$, and $x_3=(2,1)$ in class $-1$. Its weight vector is $w=(1,2)$. Find the weights $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$.
steps: Only the three support vectors have $\alpha>0$. So $w=\alpha_1(2,2)+\alpha_2(4,1)-\alpha_3(2,1)=(1,2)$. The minus sign is there because $x_3$ is in class $-1$.
Balance: $\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$ gives $\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\alpha_3=0$, so $\alpha_3=\alpha_1+\alpha_2$.
First coordinate: $2\alpha_1+4\alpha_2-2\alpha_3=1$. Replace $\alpha_3$: $2\alpha_1+4\alpha_2-2\alpha_1-2\alpha_2=2\alpha_2=1$. So $\alpha_2=0.5$.
Second coordinate: $2\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\alpha_3=2$. Replace $\alpha_3$: $2\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\alpha_1-\alpha_2=\alpha_1=2$. Then $\alpha_3=2+0.5=2.5$.
examples.answer: $\alpha=(2,\ 0.5,\ 2.5)$. The $+$ side total $2+0.5$ equals the $-$ side total $2.5$, and $\sum\alpha=\|w\|^2=5$.

examples.setup: For the same three support vectors, three students propose dual weights: P $(2,1,2)$, Q $(1,1,2)$, R $(2,0.5,2.5)$. The trained $w$ is $(1,2)$. Which can be right? Use the quick filters $\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$, $w=\sum\alpha_iy_ix_i$ and $\sum\alpha_i=\|w\|^2$.
steps: P: $\sum\alpha_iy_i=2+1-2=1\ne0$. The classes do not balance. Rejected.
Q: $\sum\alpha_iy_i=1+1-2=0$, so it passes the balance test. Then $w=1(2,2)+1(4,1)-2(2,1)=(2,2)+(4,1)-(4,2)=(2,1)$. That is not $(1,2)$. Also $\sum\alpha=4$ but $\|w\|^2=5$. Rejected.
examples.answer: Only R. The balance condition and $\sum\alpha=\|w\|^2$ are fast filters, and the sum $w=\sum\alpha_iy_ix_i$ is the final test.

examples.setup: A new training point $(5,4)$ with label $+1$ is added to the data above. What is its $\alpha$, and does $w$ change?

Complementary slackness: $\alpha\,(yf-1)=0$. Since $yf-1=7\ne0$, $\alpha=0$.

check.q: Two class $+1$ support vectors have $\alpha=1$ and $\alpha=3$. The only class $-1$ support vector has weight $c$. Find $c$ and $\|w\|^2$.
check.a: Balance: $1+3-c=0$, so $c=4$. Then $\|w\|^2=\sum\alpha=1+3+4=8$.

check.q: A hard-margin SVM has $\sum\alpha_i=2$. What is its margin width?

cards.title: Linear separability and XOR
cards.simple: Can you split two groups of dots with one straight ruler line? If yes, the SVM can find the widest street between them. If not, such as a red dot inside a ring of blue dots, or red on two opposite corners of a square, no ruler line will do. A quick test is to stretch a rubber band around each group. If the two bands touch or cross, no straight line can separate them. In exam words: the classes are linearly separable only if their convex hulls do not overlap. XOR is not.
cards.idea: A hard-margin linear SVM exists only if one straight line (a plane in more dimensions) can put every $+$ point on one side and every $-$ point on the other. This is **linear separability**. A quick test: stretch a rubber band, the **convex hull**, around each class. If the two bands do not touch, a line exists. If one class sits inside the other's band, or the classes sit on opposite corners (XOR), no line works.
cards.definition:
$$\text{separable}\iff\exists\,(w,b):\ y_i\,(w^\top x_i+b)>0\ \text{for all } i\iff \operatorname{conv}(+)\cap\operatorname{conv}(-)=\varnothing$$

Symbols: $\operatorname{conv}$ is the convex hull, the smallest shape with straight sides that contains the points. It is the rubber band. $\cap$ is the overlap of the two bands and $\varnothing$ means there is none.
cards.intuition_full: Why does the rubber-band test work? Suppose a point $p$ lies in both bands. A point in the $+$ band is an average of $+$ points. Every $+$ point has score above 0, and an average of positive numbers is positive, so $f(p)>0$. The same point is an average of $-$ points, so $f(p)<0$. It cannot be both, so no plane exists. In the other direction, if the bands are apart, take the two nearest points on them and draw the perpendicular bisector. That is just the margin construction of the SVM. In the XOR picture the segment joining the two $+$ points and the segment joining the two $-$ points cross in the middle, so the bands share a point. Another way to see it: XOR means 'the two inputs differ', and one weighted sum compared with one threshold cannot say that. When the classes are not separable there are two cures. The soft margin accepts a few mistakes. A feature map adds a new coordinate, such as $(x_1-3)(x_2-3)$, so that the classes become separable.

examples.setup: Four points: class $+1$ at $(1,1)$ and $(5,5)$, class $-1$ at $(1,5)$ and $(5,1)$. Can a hard-margin linear SVM separate them? If not, what helps?
steps: We need one line with both $+$ points on one side and both $-$ points on the other.
Try $x_1=3$. Each side holds one $+$ and one $-$. Other lines also leave a mix. The best a line can do is 3 of 4 correct.
Rubber band around $+$: the segment from $(1,1)$ to $(5,5)$. Rubber band around $-$: the segment from $(1,5)$ to $(5,1)$.

The two segments cross at $(3,3)$, the midpoint of both. The bands overlap, so no line separates the classes. A point that is an average of $+$ points needs $f>0$ and an average of $-$ points needs $f<0$.
examples.answer: Not linearly separable, because the two bands cross at $(3,3)$. No hard-margin linear SVM exists. With the extra feature $z$ they become separable.

steps: (i) The $+$ points have $x_1+x_2\le3$ and the $-$ points have $x_1+x_2\ge8$. The line $x_1+x_2=5.5$ separates them. Yes.
(ii) $(3,3)$ is the midpoint of $(2,3)$ and $(4,3)$, so it lies inside the $-$ band. The $-$ points surround it. No.
(iii) The two $+$ points sit on one diagonal and the two $-$ points on the other, so the segments cross. This is XOR. No.
(iv) The $+$ points have $x_2-x_1=3,3,4$, all positive. The $-$ points have $-3,-3,-4$, all negative. The line $x_2=x_1$ separates them. Yes.
examples.answer: (i) and (iv). Count nothing and test the bands: an enclosed point ((ii)) or crossing diagonals ((iii)) rule a data set out.

examples.setup: Three points on a line: class $+1$ at $(1,1)$, class $-1$ at $(2,2)$, class $+1$ at $(3,3)$. Is this separable? What feature fixes it?
steps: $(2,2)$ is the midpoint of the two $+$ points, so it lies inside the $+$ band. The bands overlap, so no line separates them, even with only three points.
Look at the coordinate $x_1=1,2,3$ and use the new feature $z=(x_1-2)^2$. The values are $1,0,1$.
The $-$ point now has $z=0$ and the $+$ points have $z=1$. A threshold at $z=0.5$ separates them.
examples.answer: Not separable in the original coordinates. The squared feature $(x_1-2)^2$ makes it separable. This is the 1D version of the kernel idea on a later card.

how: Picture a rubber band around each class.
Look for a shared point: one class inside the other's band, or two segments crossing.
If the bands are apart, a separating line exists. For small data a diagonal or a vertical line usually works.
If they overlap, a hard-margin linear SVM does not exist. Use a soft margin or a feature map.
cards.mistake: Judging by how many points fall on each side, or by whether the classes look balanced. One enclosed point or one crossing pair is enough to break separability. Test the bands, not the counts.
edge_cases: If the two bands only touch, there is no strictly separating line, so the hard margin has no answer.
A single point inside the other class's band makes the whole data set non-separable.
More dimensions can help: data that overlap in 2D can be separable after adding a feature.
XOR is solved by a depth-2 decision tree. Linear models cannot reach 100% on it.
connections: Logistic regression has the same separability test. The Linear separability card there shows what goes wrong with the fit.

cards.title: Soft margin and C
cards.simple: Real data is messy, so sometimes you cannot draw a clean road between the two groups. The soft margin lets a few kids stand inside the road, but each one costs you a fine, and the fine per kid is C. If the fine is huge, you squeeze the road narrow and fight to keep everyone out. If it is small, you make the road wide and let a few kids stand on it. In exam words: minimise $\tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum\xi_i$. Large $C$ is close to the hard margin and small $C$ gives a wide, forgiving margin.
cards.idea: Real data is rarely separable. The **soft margin** lets some points break the rules, at a price. Each point gets a **slack** $\xi\ge0$, the amount by which it falls short of the street edge. The SVM minimises the street cost $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ plus $C$ times the total slack. $C$ is the price per unit of slack. A big $C$ makes violations expensive, so the street is narrow and strict. A small $C$ makes them cheap, so the street is wide and forgiving.
cards.definition:
$$\min_{w,b,\xi}\ \tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i\,(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1-\xi_i,\ \ \xi_i\ge0$$

In practice $\xi_i=\max\big(0,\ 1-y_if(x_i)\big)$. Reading it: $\xi=0$ when the point is on or outside its street edge. $0<\xi<1$ means inside the street but on the correct side. $\xi=1$ means exactly on the plane. $\xi>1$ means misclassified. $C>0$ is the price of one unit of slack.
cards.intuition_full: Two forces pull on $w$. The first term $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ wants a wide street, which means a short $w$. The second term $C\sum\xi_i$ wants no point inside the street. $C$ decides who wins. If $C$ is huge, even a small violation is costly, so the SVM acts like the hard margin and bends the plane to fit every noisy point. If $C$ is tiny, violations are almost free, so the street grows until it swallows many points and the model underfits. Slack measures how far a point falls short, in units of $f$. A $+$ point with $f=0.5$ is halfway to its edge, so $\xi=0.5$. At $f=0$ it is on the plane and $\xi=1$. At $f=-0.5$ it is on the wrong side and $\xi=1.5$. Compare with ridge regression. There the penalty is $\lambda\|w\|^2$ and a big $\lambda$ means strong regularisation. Here $C$ multiplies the data-fit term, so it acts like $1/\lambda$ and a small $C$ means strong regularisation.

examples.setup: Five points on a line: class $-1$ at $x=0,1,2.5$ and class $+1$ at $x=3,4$. Compare two candidate classifiers. A: $w=4$, $b=-11$. B: $w=1$, $b=-2.5$. Which has the lower soft-margin cost $\tfrac12w^2+C\sum\xi$ at $C=2$, and at $C=10$?
steps: The $-$ at 2.5 sits right next to the $+$ at 3. They are only 0.5 apart.
A: $f=4x-11$. $f(2.5)=-1$ and $f(3)=1$, so every point has $yf\ge1$ and all slacks are 0. Cost $=\tfrac12\cdot16=8$.
B: $f=x-2.5$. $f(2.5)=0$, so $yf=0$ and $\xi=1$. $f(3)=0.5$, so $\xi=1-0.5=0.5$. The other points have $yf\ge1.5$, so $\xi=0$. $\sum\xi=1.5$ and $\tfrac12w^2=0.5$.
$C=2$: A costs $8+2\cdot0=8$. B costs $0.5+2\cdot1.5=3.5$. B is cheaper.
$C=10$: A still costs 8. B costs $0.5+10\cdot1.5=15.5$. A is cheaper.
examples.answer: At $C=2$ the wide street B wins (3.5 against 8). At $C=10$ the narrow street A wins (8 against 15.5). Larger $C$ pushes toward fewer violations and a narrower margin.

examples.setup: A soft-margin SVM has $w=(1,2)$, $b=-1.5$ and $C=2$. Points: $+1$ at $(1,1),(2,0),(3,0)$; $-1$ at $(0,1),(0,0),(-1,1)$. Find every slack, the objective, and the number of misclassified points.
steps: Misclassified means $yf<0$, which is $\xi>1$: only $(0,1)$ with $\xi=1.5$.

cards.why: $C$ is the one knob of a linear SVM. It sets the balance between a wide margin and few violations. In GATE: say what happens to the margin, the violations and the support vectors when $C$ changes, or compute the objective from given $w$, $C$ and slacks.
how: For each point compute the slack $\xi=\max(0,\,1-y f(x))$.
Add up the slacks.
Objective $=\tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\cdot\sum\xi$.
Role of $C$: big $C$ means violations cost a lot, so the street is narrow. Small $C$ means a wide street.
cards.mistake: Reading $C$ as the cost of the margin. It is the cost of slack. A small $C$ makes violations cheap, so the margin gets wider, not stricter. A large $C$ is the strict, hard-margin-like setting.
edge_cases: $C\to\infty$ approaches the hard margin. On non-separable data it then has no good solution.
$C\to0$ makes slack almost free. The street grows and the model underfits.
Slack levels: $\xi=0$ outside or on the edge, $0<\xi<1$ inside the street on the correct side, $\xi=1$ on the plane, $\xi>1$ misclassified.
Support vectors now include points inside the street and misclassified points. Their weight $\alpha$ is capped at $C$.
connections: Ridge regression: the same push and pull between a simple model and a good fit. $C$ behaves like $1/\lambda$, so small $C$ is strong regularisation.
Bias and variance: small $C$ raises bias and lowers variance. Large $C$ does the opposite.
Cross-validation is the usual way to choose $C$.

check.q: A soft-margin SVM has $w=(2,0)$, $C=3$ and slacks $0.5,\ 0,\ 1$. What is the objective?
check.a: $\tfrac12\|w\|^2=\tfrac12\cdot4=2$. $C\sum\xi=3\cdot1.5=4.5$. Total $=6.5$.

check.q: A point has $y f=0.3$. What is its slack and where is it?
check.a: $\xi=1-0.3=0.7$. It is inside the street, but on the correct side of the plane.

check.q: You raise $C$ a lot. Does the margin get wider or narrower?
check.a: Narrower. Violations cost more, so the SVM squeezes the street to keep points out of it.

cards.title: Kernels and feature maps
cards.simple: Imagine red and blue marbles on a ruler, blue in the middle and red at both ends. No single cut on the ruler separates them. Now lift every marble by the square of its position, so far-away marbles rise high and middle ones stay low. A flat sheet at the right height now splits red from blue. A kernel is a shortcut for this lifting. It tells the SVM how similar two marbles are in the lifted world without ever lifting them. In exam words: a feature map $\phi$ lifts the data, and the kernel $K(x,z)=\phi(x)^\top\phi(z)$ gives the inner products directly.
cards.idea: When no straight line separates the classes, **lift the data** into more coordinates and look for a line there. The lift is a feature map $\phi$. A **kernel** $K(x,z)=\phi(x)^\top\phi(z)$ gives the dot product of two lifted points straight from the original points, so the SVM never builds $\phi(x)$. A straight boundary in the lifted space is a curved boundary back in the original space.
cards.definition:
$$K(x,z)=\phi(x)^\top\phi(z),\qquad K(x,z)=(x^\top z+1)^p,\qquad K(x,z)=\exp\!\big(-\gamma\,\|x-z\|^2\big)$$

The dual uses the data only through inner products, so replace every $x_i^\top x_j$ by $K(x_i,x_j)$. The classifier becomes $f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_iy_iK(x_i,x)+b$. Symbols: $\phi$ lifts a point to a longer vector. $p$ is the polynomial degree. $\gamma>0$ sets how fast similarity fades with distance.
cards.intuition_full: Why does lifting help? Lines are simple, but a line in a bigger space can look curved when you bring it back. In the example the lifted points $(x,x^2)$ lie on a parabola. A horizontal line cuts the parabola in two places. Back on the number line that is two thresholds, a boundary no single threshold could give. Why a kernel? Lifting to a large space is expensive. For $(x^\top z+1)^2$ on 2D points the lifted vector already has 6 numbers, and it grows quickly with more inputs or higher powers. But the dot product of two lifted vectors equals a quick formula on the original points, so we never build the vectors. The RBF kernel goes further. Its lifted space has infinitely many coordinates, so you cannot write $\phi$ down, yet $K$ is trivial to compute. A larger space is more flexible and can overfit, so the soft margin and cross-validation still matter. Small $\gamma$ gives smooth boundaries and large $\gamma$ gives wiggly ones that chase noise.

examples.setup: One-dimensional data: class $+1$ at $x=-3$ and $3$, class $-1$ at $x=-1,0,1$. No threshold separates them. Use the map $\phi(x)=(x,x^2)$ and find the max-margin boundary, then compute $K(3,-1)$.
steps: The $+$ points lie on both outer sides of the $-$ points, so no single threshold works.
In the lifted plane the $+$ points are at height 9 and the $-$ points at height at most 1. The best line is $x^2=5$, halfway between 1 and 9, and the margin is $9-1=8$.
Back in 1D, $x^2=5$ means $x=\pm\sqrt5\approx\pm2.24$. The classifier says $+$ outside these thresholds and $-$ between them.
Kernel: $K(x,z)=\phi(x)^\top\phi(z)=xz+x^2z^2$. For $x=3$, $z=-1$: $(3,9)\cdot(-1,1)=-3+9=6$, and the formula gives $-3+9=6$.
examples.answer: Boundary at $x=\pm\sqrt5$ (lifted margin 8), and $K(3,-1)=6$. A linear method in the lifted space gave a non-linear boundary in 1D.

examples.setup: Polynomial kernel $K(x,z)=(x^\top z+1)^2$ on the 2D points $x=(2,1)$ and $z=(1,3)$. Compute $K(x,z)$ from the formula, then check it against the lifted vectors $\phi(x)=(x_1^2,\ x_2^2,\ \sqrt2x_1x_2,\ \sqrt2x_1,\ \sqrt2x_2,\ 1)$.
steps: Formula: $x^\top z=2\cdot1+1\cdot3=5$. So $K=(5+1)^2=36$.
Products: $4\cdot1=4$, $1\cdot9=9$, $2\sqrt2\cdot3\sqrt2=12$, $2\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=4$, $\sqrt2\cdot3\sqrt2=6$, $1\cdot1=1$. Sum $=4+9+12+4+6+1=36$.
examples.answer: 36 both ways. The formula needs one dot product. The lifted route needs six products and a 6-number vector for every point. That saving is the kernel trick.

examples.setup: RBF kernel $K(x,z)=\exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)$ with $\gamma=0.1$. Compute $K$ for $x=(2,1)$ and $z=(1,3)$, for $K(x,x)$, and for a far point $z'=(12,1)$.
steps: $K(x,x)$: the distance is 0, so $K=\exp(0)=1$.
examples.answer: $0.607$, $1$ and about $0.00005$. The RBF value is a similarity between 0 and 1. There is no finite $\phi$ for it, so the kernel is the only way to work with it.

cards.title: Valid kernels
cards.simple: A kernel is a similarity score between two items, but not every score is allowed. It must behave like a dot product of lifted points, so it gives the same answer both ways round and never acts like a negative length. Every table of scores built from it must pass a check called PSD. You do not test this each time: adding or multiplying kernels, or scaling by a positive number, keeps you safe. Subtracting does not. In exam words: $K$ is valid if it is symmetric and every Gram matrix is positive semidefinite, meaning all eigenvalues are at least 0.
cards.idea: A kernel is a dot product in disguise, so it must act like one. It must be **symmetric**, and every table of scores it produces (a **Gram matrix**) must be **positive semidefinite** (PSD), which means no negative eigenvalues. Instead of testing each time, build kernels from safe parts. Sums, products and positive multiples of kernels are kernels. A difference is not guaranteed to be one.
cards.definition:
$$K\ \text{valid}\iff K(x,z)=K(z,x)\ \text{ and every Gram matrix } G_{ij}=K(x_i,x_j)\ \text{is PSD}$$

PSD means $v^\top Gv\ge0$ for every vector $v$, which is the same as every eigenvalue of $G$ being at least 0. For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$ it means $a\ge0$, $c\ge0$ and $ac-b^2\ge0$. Safe rules: if $K_1,K_2$ are valid, so are $K_1+K_2$, $K_1K_2$, $cK_1$ for $c\ge0$, $(K_1+c)^p$ for $c\ge0$, and $f(x)f(z)$ for any function $f$. Not guaranteed: $K_1-K_2$.
cards.intuition_full: A valid kernel is $K(x,z)=\phi(x)^\top\phi(z)$ for some lift $\phi$. Dot products are symmetric. A vector dotted with itself is a length squared, so $K(x,x)=\|\phi(x)\|^2\ge0$. For any weights $v_i$ we get $\sum_{i,j}v_iv_jK(x_i,x_j)=\|\sum_iv_i\phi(x_i)\|^2\ge0$. That is the PSD condition in one line. Quick fail test: any negative entry on the diagonal kills the kernel. Why the safe rules work: a sum of kernels joins the two feature vectors end to end and the dot products add. A product uses all pairwise products of features. $f(x)f(z)$ is a one-number feature map $\phi=f$. Why subtraction is risky: taking away a kernel can push a diagonal entry below zero, and a squared length cannot be negative. Passing the diagonal test is not enough on its own. $K(x,z)=x^2+z^2$ has non-negative diagonal $2x^2$, but its Gram matrix on $0,1$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $-1$.

examples.setup: Test $K(x,z)=2xz+3$ on the points $x=1$ and $x=2$. Is it a valid kernel? Then test $K'(x,z)=3-2xz$.
steps: The Gram matrix is the table of $K(x_i,x_j)$ for the two points.
$K(1,1)=2+3=5$. $K(1,2)=K(2,1)=4+3=7$. $K(2,2)=8+3=11$. The table $\begin{pmatrix}5&7\\7&11\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric.
$\det=5\cdot11-7\cdot7=55-49=6\ge0$ and the diagonal entries are positive, so it is PSD. The eigenvalues are $8\pm\sqrt{58}\approx15.62$ and $0.38$, both positive.
Build-up check: $2xz$ is twice the linear kernel and $3=f(x)f(z)$ with $f=\sqrt3$. A sum of kernels is a kernel. Valid.
For $K'=3-2xz$: $K'(1,1)=1$, $K'(1,2)=-1$, $K'(2,2)=3-8=-5$. The diagonal entry $-5<0$ and $\det=-5-1=-6<0$. Not PSD, so $K'$ is not a kernel.
examples.answer: $2xz+3$ is valid and $3-2xz$ is not. A negative diagonal entry or a negative determinant settles it.

examples.setup: The expression $K_0(x,z)=f(x)g(z)+f(z)g(x)$ with $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2$ is not a valid kernel. Which extra term makes it valid?
steps: Check the diagonal: $K_0(x,x)=2x\cdot x^2=2x^3$. At $x=-1$ it is $-2<0$, so $K_0$ is not valid.
Let $h=f+g$, so $h(x)=x+x^2$. Expand $h(x)h(z)=f(x)f(z)+f(x)g(z)+g(x)f(z)+g(x)g(z)$.
The two middle terms are exactly $K_0$. So adding $f(x)f(z)+g(x)g(z)=xz+x^2z^2$ gives $K_0+xz+x^2z^2=h(x)h(z)$.
Spot check at $x=1$, $z=2$: $K_0=1\cdot4+1\cdot2=6$. Adding $xz+x^2z^2=2+4$ gives 12, and $h(1)h(2)=2\cdot6=12$.
$h(x)h(z)$ is a kernel: it is $\phi(x)^\top\phi(z)$ with the one-number map $\phi=h$. Its Gram matrix is $hh^\top$, which is PSD.
examples.answer: Add $f(x)f(z)+g(x)g(z)=xz+x^2z^2$. The result is $h(x)h(z)$, a perfect square of the form $\phi^\top\phi$.

examples.setup: $K_1(x,z)=3xz$ and $K_2(x,z)=xz$ are both valid. Is $K_1-K_2$ valid? Is $K_2-K_1$?
steps: $K_1-K_2=3xz-xz=2xz$. That is twice the linear kernel, so it is valid.
$K_2-K_1=xz-3xz=-2xz$. On the diagonal at $x=1$: $-2<0$. Not valid.
examples.answer: $K_1-K_2$ is valid and $K_2-K_1$ is not. So a difference is not guaranteed to be a kernel: sometimes it works and sometimes it does not. A question that says 'which is NOT guaranteed to be a kernel' points to the difference.

cards.why: Kernel validity is the one place where an SVM question turns into a small linear algebra question. In GATE: say which expression is a valid kernel, or find the term that repairs an invalid one.
how: Check symmetry: $K(x,z)=K(z,x)$.
Quick fail: any $K(x,x)<0$ means invalid.
Try to build it from safe parts: sums, products, positive multiples, $f(x)f(z)$, $(xz+c)^p$ with $c\ge0$.
If unsure, write a $2\times2$ Gram matrix and test the determinant, or find its eigenvalues.
cards.mistake: Assuming $K_1-K_2$ is a kernel because $K_1$ and $K_2$ are. Subtraction can make the Gram matrix indefinite. Sums, products and positive multiples are the safe moves.
edge_cases: A negative diagonal entry $K(x,x)<0$ rules the kernel out at once.
Passing the diagonal test is not enough. $x^2+z^2$ has a non-negative diagonal but is not PSD.
A difference can be valid by luck ($3xz-xz=2xz$) but is never guaranteed.
A squared distance $\|x-z\|^2$ is not a kernel. Its Gram matrix on $0,1$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $-1$.
connections: Linear algebra: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors covers why PSD means non-negative eigenvalues, and Matrices and determinants covers the $2\times2$ determinant.
Linear algebra: Projection, orthogonality and quadratic forms covers $v^\top Gv\ge0$.
Previous card: $K=\phi^\top\phi$ is the reason these rules hold.

check.q: Is $K(x,z)=x^2+z^2$ a valid kernel? Test the points $0$ and $1$.
check.a: No. The Gram matrix on $0,1$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $0\cdot2-1=-1<0$.

check.q: Is $K(x,z)=(xz+2)^3$ valid?
check.a: Yes. $xz+2$ is the linear kernel plus a constant $\ge0$, which is valid, and a power of a kernel is a product of kernels.

check.q: Can $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ be a Gram matrix of a kernel?
check.a: No. $\det=1-4=-3<0$, so it is not PSD.

cards.what: A kernel is a dot product in disguise, so it must act like one. It must be **symmetric**, and every table of scores it produces (a **Gram matrix**) must be **positive semidefinite** (PSD), which means no negative eigenvalues. Instead of testing each time, build kernels from safe parts. Sums, products and positive multiples of kernels are kernels. A difference is not guaranteed to be one.
cards.what_full:
A kernel is a dot product in disguise, so it must act like one. It must be **symmetric**, and every table of scores it produces (a **Gram matrix**) must be **positive semidefinite** (PSD), which means no negative eigenvalues. Instead of testing each time, build kernels from safe parts. Sums, products and positive multiples of kernels are kernels. A difference is not guaranteed to be one.

$$K\ \text{valid}\iff K(x,z)=K(z,x)\ \text{ and every Gram matrix } G_{ij}=K(x_i,x_j)\ \text{is PSD}$$

PSD means $v^\top Gv\ge0$ for every vector $v$, which is the same as every eigenvalue of $G$ being at least 0. For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$ it means $a\ge0$, $c\ge0$ and $ac-b^2\ge0$. Safe rules: if $K_1,K_2$ are valid, so are $K_1+K_2$, $K_1K_2$, $cK_1$ for $c\ge0$, $(K_1+c)^p$ for $c\ge0$, and $f(x)f(z)$ for any function $f$. Not guaranteed: $K_1-K_2$.

**Worked example.** Test $K(x,z)=2xz+3$ on the points $x=1$ and $x=2$. Is it a valid kernel? Then test $K'(x,z)=3-2xz$.

1. The Gram matrix is the table of $K(x_i,x_j)$ for the two points.
2. $K(1,1)=2+3=5$. $K(1,2)=K(2,1)=4+3=7$. $K(2,2)=8+3=11$. The table $\begin{pmatrix}5&7\\7&11\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric.
3. $\det=5\cdot11-7\cdot7=55-49=6\ge0$ and the diagonal entries are positive, so it is PSD. The eigenvalues are $8\pm\sqrt{58}\approx15.62$ and $0.38$, both positive.
4. Build-up check: $2xz$ is twice the linear kernel and $3=f(x)f(z)$ with $f=\sqrt3$. A sum of kernels is a kernel. Valid.
5. For $K'=3-2xz$: $K'(1,1)=1$, $K'(1,2)=-1$, $K'(2,2)=3-8=-5$. The diagonal entry $-5<0$ and $\det=-5-1=-6<0$. Not PSD, so $K'$ is not a kernel.

**Answer:** $2xz+3$ is valid and $3-2xz$ is not. A negative diagonal entry or a negative determinant settles it.

**Check yourself:** Is $K(x,z)=x^2+z^2$ a valid kernel? Test the points $0$ and $1$.

*Answer:* No. The Gram matrix on $0,1$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $0\cdot2-1=-1<0$.

scenes.title: Score and distance of a point from the plane

steps.caption: The plane is 5x1 + 12x2 - 30 = 0, so w = (5, 12) and b = -30. The length of w is |w| = sqrt(25 + 144) = 13.
Point A = (4, 3). Its score is f(A) = 20 + 36 - 30 = 26. Positive, so A is on the + side.
Distance of A = |f| / |w| = 26 / 13 = 2. The dashed segment meets the plane at a right angle and is 2 long.
Point B = (1, 1). Its score is f(B) = 5 + 12 - 30 = -13. Negative, so B is on the - side. Its distance is 13 / 13 = 1.
A is 2 away on the + side and B is 1 away on the - side. The score 26 is not a distance: divide by 13 first.

scenes.title: Hard margin from two points: width 2/|w|

steps.caption: Two points: + at (4, 6) and - at (1, 2). The rule y f(x) >= 1 needs f(4, 6) >= 1 and f(1, 2) <= -1. The best plane makes both exactly tight.
The two points are the nearest pair, so w points along d = (4, 6) - (1, 2) = (3, 4). Its length is |d| = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5.
f has to climb from -1 to +1, a rise of 2, across a distance of 5. The climb per unit step is |w|, so |w| = 2/5 = 0.4. The street width is 2/|w| = 5.

set.text: f rises by 2 over a distance of 5

steps.caption: w has length 0.4 and the direction of d, which is d/|d| = (0.6, 0.8). So w = 0.4 x (0.6, 0.8) = (0.24, 0.32).

scenes.title: Support vectors sit on the edge of the street

steps.caption: Trained plane: x1 - 2 x2 - 1 = 0, so w = (1, -2) and b = -1. The dashed lines are f = +1 and f = -1. Three + points and three - points.
The support vectors are the points with y f = 1 exactly. They sit on the dashed lines: (4,1), (6,2) and (4,2). The other three have y f above 1.
Delete the three far points and retrain. The plane and the street do not move, so only the support vectors matter.

scenes.title: w is built from support vectors, each scaled by its weight

objects.text: w = α1 x1 + α2 x2 - α3 x3

steps.caption: The trained SVM has support vectors x1 = (2,2) and x2 = (4,1) in class +, x3 = (2,1) in class -, and w = (1,2). The weight vector is built from them: w = a1 x1 + a2 x2 - a3 x3. We want the weights a (alpha).
The two classes must pull equally: a1 + a2 - a3 = 0, so a3 = a1 + a2. This removes one unknown.
First coordinate of w: 2 a1 + 4 a2 - 2 a3 = 1. Put a3 = a1 + a2: 2 a1 + 4 a2 - 2 a1 - 2 a2 = 2 a2 = 1. So a2 = 0.5 and the vector 0.5 x2 = (2, 0.5) is the first step.
Second coordinate: 2 a1 + a2 - a3 = 2, which becomes a1 = 2. Then a3 = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5. Add 2 x1 = (4,4), then subtract 2.5 x3 = (5, 2.5).
The three steps end at (1, 2) = w. Check: the weights sum to 2 + 0.5 + 2.5 = 5, and |w|^2 = 1 + 4 = 5.

scenes.title: XOR points: overlapping rubber bands mean no separating line

steps.caption: Four points: + at (1,1) and (5,5), - at (1,5) and (5,1). Can one straight line put both + on one side and both - on the other?
Try the vertical line x1 = 3. Each side holds one + and one -. Any other line leaves a mix too. The best a line can do is 3 of 4 right.

set.text: x1 = 3 leaves a mix on both sides

steps.caption: Stretch a rubber band around each class. The + band is the segment from (1,1) to (5,5). The - band is the segment from (1,5) to (5,1).
The two bands cross at (3,3). A point in both bands would be an average of + points and an average of - points, so its score would be both positive and negative. No line can separate the classes.
Add the feature z = (x1-3)(x2-3). The two + points get z = 4 and 4, the two - points get z = -4 and -4. The sign of z now separates the classes.

scenes.title: Soft margin: small C picks a wide street, large C a narrow one

steps.caption: Five points on a line. The - points are at 0, 1 and 2.5. The + points are at 3 and 4. The - at 2.5 sits right next to the + at 3.
Candidate A is a hard margin: street edges at 2.5 and 3. f must rise by 2 over a gap of 0.5, so w = 4 and b = -11. Cost: half of w squared is 8, slack is 0.

set.text: A: narrow street, no point inside

steps.caption: Candidate B is a wide street: w = 1, b = -2.5, edges at 1.5 and 3.5. The - at 2.5 is on the boundary (y f = 0, slack 1). The + at 3 is inside the street (y f = 0.5, slack 0.5). Slack total 1.5, and half of w squared is 0.5.

set.text: B: wide street, two points inside

steps.caption: Take C = 2. Cost A = 8 + 2 x 0 = 8. Cost B = 0.5 + 2 x 1.5 = 3.5. B is cheaper, so a small C prefers the wide street.

set.text: C = 2: the wide street B wins

steps.caption: Take C = 10. Cost A is still 8. Cost B = 0.5 + 10 x 1.5 = 15.5. Now A is cheaper, so a large C prefers the narrow street.

set.text: C = 10: the narrow street A wins

scenes.title: A feature map makes data separable; the kernel is its dot product

steps.caption: One-dimensional data: + at -3 and 3, - at -1, 0 and 1. The + points sit on both outer sides, so no single threshold on the line separates them.
Lift each point to (x, x²). The outer points rise to height 9. The inner points stay low, at heights 1, 0 and 1.
Now a horizontal line splits the classes. The street runs from height 1 to height 9, so the best line is x² = 5 and the margin is 9 - 1 = 8. A linear SVM can find it.
Back on the number line, x² = 5 means x = -√5 or x = √5, about ±2.24. A linear method has produced two thresholds, a non-linear boundary.
The kernel is a shortcut. K(x, z) = φ(x)·φ(z) = xz + x²z². For x = 3 and z = -1 it gives 6, the same as the dot product of (3, 9) and (-1, 1). The SVM only ever needs K.

scenes.title: Gram matrix test: a valid kernel gives a PSD table

steps.caption: Is K(x, z) = 2xz + 3 a valid kernel? Test it on the two points x = 1 and x = 2. Its Gram matrix is the 2 by 2 table of all K values.
Fill the table. K(1,1) = 2 + 3 = 5. K(1,2) = 4 + 3 = 7 and K(2,1) = 7. K(2,2) = 8 + 3 = 11. It is symmetric.
PSD test for a 2 by 2 matrix: both diagonal entries at least 0 and det at least 0. det = 5 x 11 - 7 x 7 = 55 - 49 = 6, so it passes. The eigenvalues are about 15.62 and 0.38, both positive.
Build-up check: 2xz is a positive multiple of the linear kernel xz, and 3 = f(x)f(z) with f = √3. A sum of kernels is a kernel, so it is valid.
Now the difference K'(x, z) = 3 - 2xz. Its table is [[1, -1], [-1, -5]]. The diagonal entry -5 is negative, and det = -5 - 1 = -6. It is not PSD, so it is not a kernel.
